newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt to champion Palestinians in summit with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Egypt to champion Palestinians in summit with Israel.

text.p: Egypt has made clear it will champion the Palestinian side when President Hosni Mubarak and Israel's prime minister meet on Tuesday, but will also listen to any ideas on reviving Middle East peace.

Contradictory views on Jewish settlements on Arab land have ground Palestinian-Israeli peace talks to a halt. Mubarak will meet Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh to try to end the deadlock.
On Monday, Mubarak held talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat in Cairo to coordinate views before the meeting.

"The issue is settlements. (Tuesday's) meeting is very important because we're talking about how to remedy the flaws in the peace process on specific bases...the Oslo and Madrid peace accords," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters after the meeting.

He was referring to the 1991 Middle East peace conference in Madrid at which Israel and the Palestinians agreed to trade occupied lands for peace -- a formula Netanyahu now rejects -- and the ensuing Oslo peace accord, which could be the basis of a final peace agreement.
"Arafat has articulated his point of view to us well. We're going to talk to him (Netanyahu) and we're going to listen to what he has to say or wishes to say," Moussa added.

"The Palestinians say they cannot negotiate against a background of fait accomplis and the continuation of settlements. Our job is to deal with that in order to pave the way for the resumption of a positive atmosphere which will enable us to save the peace process."
Arafat refuses to talk peace with Israel until the Jewish state stops construction work on a new Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem.
But Netanyahu says he will not stop building Jewish settlements and that the Palestinians must put an end to extremist violence before he will negotiate with them.

The Israeli prime minister has also said the issue of settlements was not on his agenda for Tuesday's meeting with Mubarak but Moussa told reporters that Netanyahu had some views that "he has not divulged before" to discuss with Mubarak.
"There's a lot that can happen at the meeting and we hope it will lead to the resumption of the peace process," he added.

Asked if he thought either Arafat or Netanyahu would compromise, Moussa said: "We hope so, meaning Netanyahu. The question is saving the peace and peace is incompatible with changes, fait accomplis and settlements."
Moussa struck a hopeful note on its success, but the U.S. ambassador to Israel said he did not expect any breakthroughs.

"We do not expect a dramatic breakthrough...but a better understanding towards the way in which Israel, Egypt, the Palestinians and the United States will continue to advance the peace process," Israel's domestic news agency Itim quoted Martin Indyk as saying on Monday.
"We do not want failure but I caution against expectations which are too high."

The United States, which is a sponsor of the peace process, sent envoy Dennis Ross to the region earlier this month to try to end the stalemate but his mission ended in failure. Indyk said the peace process would move forward only when Israel and the PLO were ready.
"It's up to the parties themselves to take the steps necessary to put the process back on track. We'll ready to help them but we can't do it for them," Indyk told reporters.
